idiom_name: struct of function pointers (ops table) filled in per test
implementation_notes: C has no interfaces and no reflection, so the classic structure is hand-written: the collaborator role is a struct whose members are function pointers, and the module under test receives a pointer to that struct instead of calling the real functions. A reusable double is a file-local table whose fill-in functions read canned answers from variables the test sets before installing the table, which is the configuration interface in procedural form. CMock generates a double from a header, but it is a build-time tool, so plain C remains in the hand-written camp.
pitfalls: File-scope state (static variables) makes the double shared across tests: reset it in setup or return a fresh table per test.

A struct of function pointers is a plain copy; assigning a callback whose parameter list differs compiles silently, unlike a C++ virtual override, so signature drift is caught only by the compiler warning flags or at runtime.
Registering the fake through a global (a testing hook selected by a flag) instead of passing the table in is test logic in production.

variants.name: CMock generated doubles with Expect/ExpectAndReturn
variants.implementation_notes: CMock parses the dependency header and generates a mock module plus one configuration function per function prototype: foo_ExpectAndReturn(args..., value) queues a canned response together with the arguments the call must have, foo_ExpectAndThrow queues a failure, foo_StubWithCallback delegates to a per-test callback and foo_IgnoreAndReturn disables argument checking for that call. Queued calls are replayed in order and verified afterwards, so this is the statically generated route to a configurable double. It is a code generator, so the generated mock must be regenerated whenever the header changes.
pitfalls: Generated mocks drift from the header unless regeneration is wired into the build (Ceedling/Rakefile); a stale generated file keeps compiling against the old prototype.
Expectations are queued per test binary, so a test that does not drain or reset the queue leaves the double configured for the next test.
Expect is order-sensitive: using it for calls whose order is not part of the contract turns a refactoring into a failing test.
